title: NIST SP 800-137, Information Security Continuous Monitoring ...
content:
- **Source section: Executive Summary / Chapter 1 / Chapter 2 / Chapter 3 / Appendix D**
  - **Frequency/timeline explicitly stated:** “ongoing”, “continuous”, “regularly”, “as often as needed”, “on demand”, “real-time”, “near real-time”, “discrete intervals”, “periodic”, “preestablished frequency”, “higher frequencies”, “various frequencies”, “different intervals”, “at least quarterly”, “monthly”, “weekly”, “daily”, “annually”, “every minute”, “hourly”, “biweekly”, “within organizational risk tolerances”, “within X days” — **the source frequently states that frequencies are risk-based, organization-defined, or tier-defined rather than prescribing a single fixed cadence.**
  - **Quote/paraphrase:** “Security controls and organizational risks are assessed and analyzed at a frequency sufficient to support risk-based security decisions to adequately protect organization information.”  
  - **Likely families:** AU, CA, CM, IR, MA, SI, AC, IA, CP, PE

| Section | Documented cadence / timeline | Exact requirement / close paraphrase | Likely control family/control ID |
|---|---|---|---|
| Exec Summary; Ch. 1 | Ongoing / continuous | ISCM is “maintaining ongoing awareness of information security, vulnerabilities, and threats to support organizational risk management decisions.” “The terms ‘continuous’ and ‘ongoing’… mean that security controls and organizational risks are assessed and analyzed at a frequency sufficient to support risk-based security decisions.” | CA, AU, SI, CM, IR |
| Background | At a frequency appropriate to risk, but no less than annually | FISMA requires agencies to “conduct assessments of security controls at a frequency appropriate to risk, but no less than annually.” | CA |
| Background | Ongoing basis; frequency sufficient to make ongoing, risk-based decisions | OMB M-11-33 emphasizes “monitoring the security state of information systems on an ongoing basis with a frequency sufficient to make ongoing, risk-based decisions.” | CA, AU, SI |
| Ch. 2 intro | Frequencies not static; examples include annually, quarterly, monthly, daily | “Monitoring frequencies (e.g., annually, quarterly, monthly, daily) are not static, and they are not uniform across all metrics.” | CA, AU, CM, SI |
| Ch. 2 intro | At any interval | “An ISCM strategy can deliver dynamic updates of security-related data to support system authorizations conducted at any interval.” | CA, AU |
| Ch. 2.1.1 | Frequency with which metrics are monitored/reported is determined by risk tolerance | “The metrics and the frequency with which they are monitored and reported are determined by requirements to maintain operations within organizational risk tolerances.” | CA, AU, SI |
| Ch. 2.1.2 | Frequencies determined in part by mission/business priorities and measurement capabilities | “The frequencies with which Tier 2 security controls are assessed and security status and other metrics are monitored are determined in part by the objectives and priorities of the mission or business process and measurement capabilities inherent in the infrastructure.” | PM, CA, AU, SI |
| Ch. 2.1.3 | Ongoing basis | Tier 3 officials “conduct assessments and monitoring, and analyze results on an ongoing basis.” | CA, AU, SI |
| Ch. 2.2 | Reasonable assessment frequencies | “A more practical approach is to establish reasonable assessment frequencies for collecting security-related information.” | CA |
| Ch. 2.2 | Frequency sufficient to assure adequate security commensurate with risk | “The frequency of assessments should be sufficient to assure adequate security commensurate with risk…” | CA |
| Ch. 2.2 | Annually, quarterly, monthly, daily examples | “Monitoring frequencies (e.g., annually, quarterly, monthly, daily) are not static…” | CA, AU, SI, CM |
| Ch. 2.2 | Adjusted based on changing threats/vulnerabilities/incidents | “Security control assessment and monitoring frequencies… are adjusted to support changes…” and “priorities for ISCM vary and are adjusted in response to security incidents…” | CA, IR, SI, CM |
| Ch. 3 intro | Determining status monitoring frequencies and control assessment frequencies | ISCM program establishes “metrics, status monitoring frequencies, control assessment frequencies…” | CA, AU, SI, CM |
| Ch. 3.1 | Preestablished frequency audit | ISCM strategy includes “the inclusion of criteria describing the conditions that trigger a review or update of the strategy, in addition to the preestablished frequency audit.” | CA, AU, CM |
| Ch. 3.1.2 | At minimum; all controls assessed according to system security plan and NIST SP 800-53A | “At a minimum, all security controls… are assessed for effectiveness in accordance with the system security plan and the methods described in NIST SP 800-53A.” | CA |
| Ch. 3.1.2 | As often as required by organizational policy | “Assessment evidence obtained from ISCM is, at a minimum, provided to AOs as often as required by organizational policy.” | CA, AU |
| Ch. 3.1.4 | No specific cadence; sampling when full collection impractical | Sampling is discussed as a methodology; no fixed frequency. | CA |
| Ch. 3.2.1 | Hourly, daily, weekly; no more than annually for some items | Example metrics “might be computed hourly, daily, or weekly.” “Policies and procedures for network connectivity will be reviewed or revised no more than annually.” | CM, AU, CA |
| Ch. 3.2.2 | More frequently / less frequently; no fixed universal cadence | “Volatile security controls are assessed more frequently…” and “not volatile… would therefore typically require less frequent assessment.” | CA, CM, AU |
| Ch. 3.2.2 | Higher-impact systems more frequently than moderate; moderate more frequently than low | “Controls implemented on systems… high-impact are monitored more frequently than… moderate-impact… more frequently than… low-impact systems.” | CA, CM, AU |
| Ch. 3.2.2 | More frequent monitoring for critical functions | Security controls/objects that provide critical functions “are candidates for more frequent monitoring.” | CA, CM, AU, SI |
| Ch. 3.2.2 | More frequent monitoring until remediation complete | Controls with weaknesses in SAR/POA&M “are monitored more frequently until remediation of the weakness is complete.” | CA, SI, CM |
| Ch. 3.2.2 | Temporary or permanent increases to monitoring frequencies | Threat info may justify “temporary or permanent increases” to monitoring frequencies. | SI, CA, CM |
| Ch. 3.2.2 | Monthly patch cycle example; at least that often for scans | “If a specific product manufacturer provides software patches monthly, an organization might consider conducting vulnerability scans on that product at least that often.” | SI-2, RA-5, CA, CM |
| Ch. 3.2.2 | More frequent monitoring of records on nonlocal maintenance | If risk assessment identifies issues related to MA-4, “the organization considers more frequent monitoring of the records kept on nonlocal maintenance and diagnostic activities.” | MA-4, CA |
| Ch. 3.2.2 | Quarterly reporting requirement example | “If OMB policy requires quarterly reports on the number of unauthorized components detected and corrective actions taken, the organization would monitor the system for unauthorized components at least quarterly.” | CM-8, CA |
| Ch. 3.2.2 | AC-2 control element frequencies vary | AC-2 base and enhancements may have different monitoring frequencies; example says AC-2a is relatively infrequent, AC-2h more frequent, AC-2(3) relatively frequent. | AC-2 |
| Ch. 3.2.2 | Minimum frequency at mission/business tier | Tier 2 establishes “the minimum frequency with which each security control or metric is to be assessed or monitored.” | CA, AU, SI, CM |
| Ch. 3.2.2 | Greater frequency than prescribed by organization | At Tier 3, system owners may assess specific controls/metrics “with greater frequency than prescribed by the organization.” | CA, AU, SI, CM |
| Ch. 3.2.2 | Event-driven: immediate need | “Events may occur that trigger the immediate need to assess security controls or verify security status outside of requirements expressed in the ISCM strategy.” | IR, CA, SI |
| Ch. 3.2.2 | Event-driven assessments may trigger reauthorizations | “Depending on the significance of the event, an event-driven assessment may trigger one or more system reauthorizations.” | CA, AU |
| Ch. 3.2.3 | No fixed cadence; collection/delivery as needed | Architecture determines how information is collected and delivered; no specific cadence given. | CA, AU, SI |
| Ch. 3.4 | Frequency of reports | Procedures include “the frequency of reports.” No universal cadence prescribed. | AU, CA, SI |
| Ch. 3.4.2 | Annually; quarterly; monthly; every minute; hourly or daily | Risk executive “may receive a general report on all systems annually and a detailed report on specific high-impact systems quarterly.” CIO/SISO “quarterly.” AO “monthly comprehensive reports.” CIRT lead “when alerts are generated.” Network admins “dashboard… updated every minute, with summary metrics updated hourly or daily.” | AU, CA, SI, IR |
| Ch. 3.4.2 | More frequent reports for volatile/weak controls | “Organizations may consider more frequent reports for specific controls with more volatility or on controls for which there have been weaknesses or lack of compliance.” | CA, AU, SI |
| Ch. 3.4.3 | No fixed cadence; reporting on security status per policy | Security status reporting requirements define content/format/frequency. No universal cadence. | AU, CA, SI |
| Ch. 3.5 | Changes to frequency of monitoring | At Tier 3, responses may include “changes to the frequency of monitoring.” | CA, AU, SI |
| Ch. 3.6 | Review/update as needed; frequencies change with needs | “Security control assessments, security status metrics, and monitoring and assessment frequencies change in accordance with the needs of the organization.” | CA, AU, CM, SI |
| Ch. 3.6 | Weekly, biweekly, monthly example for component inventory | “If weekly assessments of component inventories over a six-month period indicate…” frequency may be reduced to “biweekly or monthly.” | CM-8, CA |
| Ch. 3.6 | Biweekly audit record analyses; increase to weekly | “If biweekly audit record analyses over a six-month period indicate increases in anomalous events… increase… audit record reviews to weekly.” | AU-6, AU-12, SI-4, IR |
| Ch. 3.6 | No fixed cadence; maturity-based, ongoing refinement | Strategy is continually refined; no fixed cadence. | CA, AU, CM, SI |
| Appendix D intro | Periodically | “It is important to understand and appreciate the need to assess the effectiveness of all security controls, particularly nontechnical security controls, periodically.” | CA, AU, CM, SI |
| App. D.1.1 | Regularly scheduled scans | SCAP-enabled vulnerability scanners “can be configured to scan connected systems at regular intervals.” | RA-5, CA, SI |
| App. D.1.1 | Continuous monitoring of vulnerability/patch management | No fixed cadence, but continuous monitoring is emphasized. | RA-5, SI-2, CA |
| App. D.1.2 | Routine log analysis | “Routine log analysis is beneficial…” No fixed cadence specified. | AU-6, SI-4 |
| App. D.1.3 | Periodic scans; real-time scans | Malware detection mechanisms can perform “periodic scans” and “real-time scans” of files. | SI-3, SI-4 |
| App. D.1.5 | More frequent monitoring of configurations; no fixed cadence | Configuration management tools monitor changes and restore settings; no universal cadence. | CM-2, CM-3, CM-6, CM-7, IA-2, IA-5, MA-5 |
| App. D.1.8 | At rest, in use, in transit | DLP tools monitor data “at rest, in use, and in transit.” No cadence stated. | AC-4, SI, SC-9, SI-12 |
| App. D.2.1 | No fixed cadence | SIEM tools analyze and correlate logs; frequency is tool/configuration dependent. | AU, SI, IR, CA |
| App. D.2.2 | Near real-time | Dashboard consolidates and communicates info “in near real-time.” | CA, AU, SI |
| App. D.2.2 | No fixed cadence; customizable | Dashboard output is customized to role/need; no fixed frequency. | CA, AU |
| App. D.3.2 | Updated at two-hour intervals | NVD XML data feeds are “updated at two-hour intervals.” | RA-5, SI, CA |
| App. D.3.2 | Scheduled rescans as new info becomes available | “As information becomes available in the NVD, systems are rescanned to reassess risk and mitigate any new vulnerabilities.” No fixed cadence beyond two-hour update interval for feeds. | RA-5, CA, SI |
| App. D.3.2 | No fixed cadence for checklists; dynamic updates | Security checklists are maintained and revised as necessary; no fixed cadence. | CM, CA, SI |
| App. D.4 | Query/fulfillment, reporting to tiers; no fixed cadence | Reference model supports reporting and risk-based decision making; no universal cadence specified. | CA, AU, SI |
| Glossary / definitions | Retention period / storage “for an appropriate period of time” | “Logs are a key resource…” and log management is essential for ensuring “security records are stored in sufficient detail for an appropriate period of time.” | AU, SI |
| Glossary / definitions | Scheduled completion dates | POA&M “details resources… milestones… and scheduled completion dates for the milestones.” | CA, SI, PM |
| Glossary / definitions | Ongoing / near real-time / real-time | Definitions of ISCM, operational security status, dashboard, etc., repeatedly use ongoing/real-time/near real-time. | CA, AU, SI, CM |

title: CMS Plan of Action and Milestones (POA&M) Handbook
content:
### CMS POA&M Handbook — documented operational cadence / frequency / timeline details

| Source section | Exact / closely paraphrased requirement | Cadence / timeline | Likely control family / ID |
|---|---|---:|---|
| **Last Reviewed / header** | “Last Reviewed: 4/5/2023” | Date stamp only | N/A |
| **POA&M process overview** | POA&Ms are tracked in CFACTS for risk management and compliance. | Ongoing | CA, CM, AU |
| **What is a POA&M?** | POA&M provides “milestones for correcting the weaknesses, and scheduled completion dates for the milestones.” | Scheduled completion dates | CA, CM, SI, AU |
| **Weakness severity levels** | “Senior management must be notified and immediate or near immediate corrective action must be taken.” (for significant deficiency) | Immediate / near-immediate | IR, CA, AU, SI |
| **Weakness severity levels** | “Corrective actions for a reportable condition may be scheduled over a longer period of time.” | Longer period of time; no specific cadence | CA, SI, AU |
| **Weakness severity levels** | Weaknesses “must be mitigated in a timely and efficient manner, as resources permit.” | Timely; no specific cadence | CA, SI |
| **Finding weaknesses** | Weaknesses may be found through “Continuous Diagnostics and Mitigation (CDM) efforts.” | Continuous | CA, SI, AU |
| **Finding weaknesses** | Sources listed include “Annual Assessments” | Annual | CA, AU, SI, CM |
| **Finding weaknesses** | Sources listed include “Vulnerability Scanning” | No explicit frequency in this section | SI, CA, AU |
| **Finding weaknesses** | Sources listed include “Penetration Testing” | No explicit frequency in this section | CA, SI, AU |
| **Proactive** | “Proactive weakness identification occurs during regular system reviews conducted by CMS.” | Regular; no specific cadence | CA, AU, CM |
| **Root Cause Analysis (RCA)** | “All weaknesses must be examined to determine their root cause prior to documentation in the POA&M.” | Before documentation | CA |
| **Prioritizing weaknesses** | Weaknesses “will normally require more immediate resolution” if on a High or Moderate system or contributing to material weakness / significant deficiency / reportable condition. | More immediate | CA, SI, AU |
| **Develop a Corrective Action Plan (CAP)** | CAP must include “a timeline for correcting the weakness including a completion date.” | Timeline / completion date | CA, CM, SI |
| **Appropriate milestones** | Milestones must be “Time-related – specify when the result(s) can be achieved.” | Time-related; no specific cadence | CA |
| **Appropriate milestones** | “Each weakness must have at least one corresponding milestone with an estimated completion date and resource requirements.” | Estimated completion date | CA |
| **Compliant milestones example: vulnerability scanning** | “Implement an ongoing process to evaluate and update the inventory, the SSPP, and the vulnerability scans on a regular basis; (3/15/2019)” | Ongoing / regular basis; no fixed interval | SI, CA, CM |
| **Compliant milestones example: audit logs** | “Audit logs are not periodically reviewed” → milestones include review policy, identify SO, training, and follow-up review. | Periodically; follow-up review date shown in example only | AU |
| **CAP entry into CFACTS** | “The status of the POA&M will automatically be moved from ‘draft’ to ‘ongoing’ 30 days after the weakness creation date.” | **30 days** after weakness creation | CA, CM |
| **CAP entry into CFACTS** | “Once a milestone has been accepted/approved and closed, the record must be retained for one year.” | **1 year** retention | AU, CA, CM |
| **Determine resource and funding availability** | Example question: “Can the task be accomplished within a week or will it take several months?” | Within a week / several months (examples only) | CA |
| **Assign a completion date** | Scheduled completion date is determined using “the remediation and mitigation timeline, the risk level, and the severity level.” | Risk/severity-based; no fixed cadence | CA, SI |
| **Assign a completion date** | “The milestone(s) completion date must not exceed the scheduled completion date assigned to the weakness.” | Completion date ceiling | CA |
| **Assign a completion date** | “The scheduled completion date established at the creation of the weakness must not be modified after the weakness is reported to OMB.” | Fixed after OMB reporting | CA |
| **Assign a completion date** | “If a weakness is not remediated within the scheduled completion date, a new estimated completion date must be determined and documented…” | Upon missing scheduled completion date | CA |
| **Execute the Corrective Action Plan (CAP)** | If milestone completion extends past original estimated completion date, “an update to the milestone and the completion date…must be captured” in CFACTS. | Upon extension past original date | CA, CM |
| **Execute the Corrective Action Plan (CAP)** | If scheduled completion date has passed, weakness must default to “Delayed” status and a justification with a new estimated completion date documented. | Upon passing scheduled completion date | CA |
| **Verify weakness completion** | “CMS requires that all information in the POA&M be updated at least quarterly” | **At least quarterly** | CA, AU, CM |
| **Verify weakness completion** | ISSO review includes validating weakness identification/prioritization, ensuring resources, and ensuring the schedule is appropriate and achievable. | Quarterly review cadence implied by update requirement | CA, AU |
| **Accept risk when applicable** | “After approval, RBDs shall be reviewed at least annually” | **At least annually** | CA, IR, AU |
| **Accept risk when applicable** | RBDs must be “updated as events occur and information changes.” | Event-driven / as-needed | CA |
| **Reports** | “CMS reports its remediation efforts on a monthly basis.” | **Monthly** | CA, AU |
| **Reports** | “CMS must submit POA&M updates at least once a month (by the 3rd business day of each month)” | **At least monthly; by 3rd business day of each month** | CA, AU |
| **Reports** | “The information in the POA&M must be maintained continuously” | Continuous | CA, CM, AU |
| **Reports** | Completed POA&Ms retained “for up to one year from the date of completion.” | **Up to 1 year** | AU, CA, CM |
| **Weakness remediation and mitigation timeline** | “Critical within 15 days” | **15 days** | CA, SI, AU |
| **Weakness remediation and mitigation timeline** | “High within 30 days” | **30 days** | CA, SI, AU |
| **Weakness remediation and mitigation timeline** | “Moderate within 90 days” | **90 days** | CA, SI, AU |
| **Weakness remediation and mitigation timeline** | “Low within 365 days” | **365 days** | CA, SI, AU |
| **Weakness remediation and mitigation timeline** | Timelines are “based on the date the weakness is identified, not the date the POA&M is created.” | Identification-date driven | CA, AU |
| **Weakness remediation and mitigation timeline** | If more time is needed, “the justification with a modified estimated completion date shall be documented…” | On extension need / before overrun | CA |
| **Weakness remediation and mitigation timeline** | If weaknesses are not remediated within scheduled completion date, “the status shall change to ‘Delayed’.” | Upon missing scheduled completion date | CA |
| **Weaknesses discovered during a government audit** | Weaknesses identified during a government audit “shall be documented in the POA&M after the audit draft report is produced.” | After draft audit report is produced | AU, CA |
| **Weaknesses discovered during a government audit** | “Systems must review and update POA&Ms at least quarterly.” | **At least quarterly** | CA, AU |
| **Weaknesses discovered during a government audit** | “Compensating controls must be in place and documented until weaknesses are remediated or mitigated to an acceptable level of risk.” | Until remediation/acceptable risk | CA, AU |
| **POA&M Glossary — Annual Assessment** | “Within every three hundred sixty-five (365) days” | **Every 365 days** | CA, AU, SI |
| **POA&M Glossary — Risk accepted** | “The weakness and corresponding risk must be monitored periodically to ensure the associated risk remains at an acceptable level.” | Periodically; no specific cadence | CA, IR |
| **POA&M Glossary — Scheduled or estimated completion date** | “A realistic estimate of the amount of time it will take to complete all associated milestones” | Estimate-based; no fixed cadence | CA |
| **POA&M Glossary — Ongoing** | “A status assigned when a weakness is in the process of being mitigated and has not yet exceeded the original scheduled completion date.” | Ongoing until scheduled date not exceeded | CA |
| **POA&M Glossary — Delayed** | “A status assigned when a weakness continues to be mitigated after the original scheduled completion date has passed.” | After scheduled date passes | CA |
| **POA&M Glossary — Pending verification** | Milestones/corrective actions completed but require review and sign-off. | Upon completion awaiting verification | CA, AU |
| **POA&M Glossary — Draft** | Weakness requires review and approval prior to official entry in POA&M. | Pre-entry / pre-approval | CA, AU |
| **POA&M Glossary — Completed** | Status when all corrective actions are completed or closed and weakness verified as successfully mitigated. | Upon completion | CA, AU |
| **POA&M Glossary — FISMA** | Requires agencies to “conduct annual IT security reviews of all programs and systems” and report results to OMB. | Annual | CA, AU, SI |

### Explicit absences / no specific cadence stated
- **Many items are risk-based or org-defined with no fixed interval given**:
  - “regular system reviews”
  - “regular basis”
  - “periodically”
  - “longer period of time”
  - “timely and efficient manner”
  - “as events occur and information changes”
- **Vulnerability scanning, penetration testing, audit-log review, and CDM** are mentioned, but **this page does not specify a fixed frequency** for those activities beyond the examples and general statements above.

title: Computer Security Incident Handling Guide
content:
### Document scope / absence of NIST SP 800-53 Rev 4 / RMF / JSIG style maintenance schedules
- **No explicit NIST SP 800-53 Rev 4 / RMF / JSIG maintenance cadence schedules are documented in this page.**
- The source is **NIST SP 800-61 Rev. 2 (Computer Security Incident Handling Guide)**, and it provides **incident-response operational guidance**, not control-implementation frequencies for **MA, CM, AU, SI, CA, CP, IR, PE, AC, IA** controls.
- Where timing appears, it is generally **incident-response process timing** or **organization-defined / risk-based** language rather than fixed control-maintenance cadences.

---

## Extracted operational cadence / frequency / timeline items

| Cadence / timeline | Exact requirement / paraphrase | Likely control family / control ID |
|---|---|---|
| **At least annually** | “Once an organization develops a plan and gains management approval, the organization should implement the plan and **review it at least annually** to ensure the organization is following the roadmap for maturing the capability and fulfilling their goals for incident response.” | **IR** (incident response plan review/maintenance); possibly **CA/CM** style maintenance, but not stated as a control |
| **24-hours-a-day, 7-days-a-week (24/7)** | “The most prevalent arrangement is for the organization to outsource **24-hours-a-day, 7-days-a-week (24/7) monitoring** of intrusion detection sensors, firewalls, and other security devices…” | **AU / SI / IR** (monitoring and incident detection); also operations support |
| **24/7 availability** | “Most organizations need incident response staff to be available **24/7**.” | **IR** |
| **Real-time availability** | “Real-time availability is the best for incident response because the longer an incident lasts, the more potential there is for damage and loss.” | **IR** |
| **At all times** | “The jump kit should be ready to go **at all times**.” | **IR / MA** (readiness/support equipment), but not a control schedule |
| **At least two computing devices per incident handler** | “Each incident handler should have access to **at least two computing devices**…” | **IR** support readiness |
| **Continually monitoring** | “Continually monitoring for attacks is essential.” | **AU / SI / IR** |
| **Regularly** | “Organizations should establish logging standards and procedures to ensure that adequate information is collected by logs and security software and that the data is reviewed **regularly**.” | **AU / SI** |
| **Frequent log reviews** | “Conducting **frequent log reviews** should keep the knowledge fresh…” | **AU** |
| **Baseline level of logging** | “Organizations should require a **baseline level of logging on all systems** and a higher baseline level on critical systems.” | **AU** |
| **Higher baseline level on critical systems** | Same sentence as above. | **AU** |
| **Periodically** | “Lessons learned meetings can also be held **periodically** for lesser incidents as time and resources permit.” | **IR** |
| **Within several days of the end of the incident** | “The meeting should be held **within several days of the end of the incident**.” | **IR** |
| **Designated intervals** | “Because of the changing nature of information technology and changes in personnel, the incident response team should review all related documentation and procedures for handling incidents at **designated intervals**.” | **IR** |
| **As soon as the team suspects that an incident has occurred** | “An incident response team that suspects that an incident has occurred should **immediately start recording all facts** regarding the incident.” | **IR** |
| **As soon as one suspects that an incident may have occurred** | “It is generally desirable to acquire evidence from a system of interest **as soon as one suspects that an incident may have occurred**.” | **IR / AU** (evidence handling / logging) |
| **Whenever evidence is transferred** | “Whenever evidence is transferred from person to person, chain of custody forms should detail the transfer and include each party’s signature.” | **IR** |
| **Each step from detection to final resolution** | “Every step taken from the time the incident was detected to its final resolution should be documented and timestamped.” | **IR** |
| **Initial notification, regular status updates** | Policy should state “what must be reported to whom and at what times (e.g., **initial notification, regular status updates**).” | **IR** |
| **Daily briefings** | “Possible communication methods include… **In person (e.g., daily briefings)**” | **IR** |
| **After a brief time—perhaps 15 minutes** | “Generally, the first step is to duplicate the initial contact. After waiting for a brief time—**perhaps 15 minutes**—the caller should escalate the incident to a higher level…” | **IR** |
| **Three years after all necessary follow-up actions have been completed** | “General Records Schedule (GRS) 24… specifies that ‘computer security incident handling, reporting and follow-up records’ should be destroyed **‘3 years after all necessary follow-up actions have been completed.’**” | **IR / AU** (records retention) |
| **Months or years after the incident ends** | “Most organizations choose to retain all evidence for **months or years after the incident ends**.” | **IR** |
| **In some cases, several years** | “If it is possible that the attacker will be prosecuted, evidence may need to be retained until all legal actions have been completed. In some cases, this may take **several years**.” | **IR** |
| **180 days** | “For example, an organization may state that email messages should be retained for only **180 days**.” | **AU / IR** (data retention context) |
| **Days to weeks** | “For large-scale incidents, recovery may take months; the intent of the early phases should be to increase the overall security with relatively quick (**days to weeks**) high value changes…” | **IR** |
